content:
I'm happy to announce that the Neukirch Uchida problem on the lean-eval now has a solution.

The Neukirch-Uchida theorem is interesting (to me) for various reasons. First, one can consider it as one of the first nontrivial theorems in anabelian geometry. In fact, the theorem predates Grothendieck's anabelian conjectures, and is probably one of the main motivations for these conjectures. Second, it is essentially the last theorem in a book that is one of the main standard references for many mathematicians working in number theory and arithmetic geometry.

One point to note here is that the proof that I autoformalized is not the proof that can be found in [NSW], and this is actually the main reason I think an autoformalization of this theorem is interesting, even in the presence of Fable 5 and GPT-5.6. The proof that I autoformalized is not written down anywhere, and I think the process itself hints to how formalization can take place at a higher level of abstraction, right now. I plan to write up a short paper explaining the proof itself, and the (auto)formalization process, which is also why the repo is still private. Below is a brief description.

First, about the proof:

  1. The classical Neukirch-Uchida proof has two main steps: a "local theory" and a "global theory". The original proof for the local theory requires local-to-global principles, class field theory, etc. And the global theory essentially requires Chebotarev's density theorem.
  2. The new proof I had in mind was for the local theory (the global theory proof was essentially the same as the one that appears in [NSW]). This modified proof doesn't actually use global class field theory, but does require a lot more abstract valuation theory and field arithmetic.
  3. Some aspects of local class field theory are still required to obtain numerical invariants for places of the number fields in question out of the absolute Galois group.

Going into this project, I knew that there were certain high-level formalization targets that had to be done to accomplish this: Chebotarev, LCFT, a paper published in the J. of Algebra from the 80s, and a modification/combination of some theorems from two of my own papers. To get started, I had GPT-5.6 write an exposition (in latex) of Chebotarev and LCFT from scratch (it did some research on its own in the process), as well as an exposition of the modification/combination of the proofs from my papers (I gave it the latex files for these papers). I then used Fable 5 to orchestrate GPT-5.6 subagents to formalize these topics, as well as the J. of Algebra paper, which eventually resulted in a formal proof of the local theory and characterization of numerical invariants needed for the proof. To finish off the proof, I followed a similar process to generate an exposition of the proof of the global theory, and to autoformalize it. Overall, the agents worked for ~3 days, using both an Anthropic and OpenAI subscription (with one usage reset for the OpenAI subscription).

I think the main surprise to me was the efficiency and persistence of models like Fable 5 and GPT-5.6. I think this formalization would have been possible with GPT-5.5 and/or Opus 4.8, but would have probably required more hands-on orchestration and certainly would have taken more than 3 days.

Finally, let me mention that formalizing the Neukirch-Uchida theorem was one of the topics that was proposed as part of the group work in this workshop. It wasn't one of the topics that ended up being worked on during the workshop, but I decided to do it anyway due to my own interest in the theorem.

Which version of chebotarev did you formalize? @Riccardo Brasca @Xavier Roblot and I autoformalised the Dirichlet version here last month and this might now be the 3rd independent formalisation :laughing:
It’s the Dirichlet-density version that was formalized.

I am becoming more and more concerned that groups who need nontrivial results such as LCFT/Cebotarev density (and more than one group needs these things) are just saying "oh the machine proved them" without specifying exactly what "them" actually is.

I think that it would be a much better outcome if these groups could write down statements of these major results and say "I have sorry-free proofs of these". I know for a fact that different people mean different things by "LCFT". Example: I need LCFT for FLT. But your message gives me no information about whether you have done what I need, or whether your interpretation of what LCFT is, is different (perhaps wildly different).

Are you able at this point to write a "LCFT Challenge" file -- not a challenge because it's already completed -- but something where you can say "here are all the definitions and theorems I formalized -- they're all sorried in this file but I have sorry-free proofs of them". That way other people will know what they can build on.

Are you envisaging this stuff ultimately ending up in Tau Ceti?

Concerning Chebotarev we have #41765 to add Dirichlet density. Once this is in mathlib there is basically only one reasonable version to state it (without changing the math). LCFT is obviously more complicated.

Riccardo Brasca said:

Once this is in mathlib there is basically only one reasonable version to state it (without changing the math).

And if this definition of Dirichlet Density isn't what Adam used then what?
Well, this could have happened three years ago with no AI involved. If mathlib changes during your work you can ignore this, change mathlib or adapt your work.

Riccardo Brasca said:

Concerning Chebotarev we have #41765 to add Dirichlet density. Once this is in mathlib there is basically only one reasonable version to state it (without changing the math). LCFT is obviously more complicated.

This is not even true -- some people interpret Cebotarev density as being a statement about natural density.

I am highlighting the ambiguity of natural language and I think this community can do better.
This is why I said "without changing the math". That is basically a different project, it's really more difficult.
It's in Cassels-Froehlich so I should think it's no problem for the machines.

If you want to see the details of the chebotarev theorem we proved, we gave the links here #PrimeNumberTheorem+ > What route to take to Chebotarev?. But yes this would be great for Tau Ceti but we need to make a roadmap.

Congratulations on the feat! Can you disclose how many LoC is the submission?
The Chebotarev in Chris's repo is apparently not in the development branch instead of master.
I'd like to mention that @David Roe was trying to verify a proposed solution to https://epoch.ai/frontiermath/open-problems/q2-absolute-galois (finding an explicit presentation of Gal⁡(Q‾p/Qp)\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_p/\mathbb{Q}_p)Gal(Q​p​/Qp​) for p=2) using Lean at the end of the LMFDB workshop (3+ weeks ago) and the status of the problem is still unresolved now: maybe a Lean formalization wasn't successful, or maybe it was successful but many gaps had to be filled so that it doesn't consistitute evidence that the AI systems had indeed solved the problem. Since the p≠2p\ne2p=2 result also appears on [NSW] and uses LCFT, maybe some cooperation could be fruitful to complete the formalization for p≠2p\ne2p=2 as well as hopefully for p=2p=2p=2.
Yes, the formalization is done and we're planning on making an announcement on Monday with details.
I agree with the statement that Fable and GPT 5.6 are big steps up from the previous models for mathematical reasoning and formalization.
I should also say that the project on Gal⁡(Q‾2/Q2)\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_2/\mathbb{Q}_2)Gal(Q​2​/Q2​) is joint with @David Turturean
@Junyan Xu — I never did any minimization for the solution, and the total LOC is ~109K.

Congratulations!

It was essentially an instance of the following handwaving that mathematicians do all the time: “if you combine this idea from this paper with that modification from that paper, then you get …”. Except it was eventually formally verified. Both of the papers were my own, but it did indeed do additional research in the process.
